rationale: Round 1 built and ran correctly, so the weights are pushed toward stronger obfuscation. The program is tiny (388 bytes of text, 3 functions), so size is effectively unconstrained; the main care point is runtime, since the sample is a compute-bound floating-point benchmark (fbench/flops/pi loops). SUB gets the highest weights because it is cheap, always applicable, and directly raises reverse-engineering effort on the dense arithmetic code. FLA and BCF are weighted high for security because control-flow flattening plus bogus predicates give the largest analysis resistance on the small set of functions, with modest RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights since the absolute overhead is tiny at this code size. ICALL and IGV are boosted for diversity — indirect calls and hidden global state disrupt static call-graph and data-flow recovery, and myadd/main give them a target. IBR is kept slightly lower on SecurityGain than FLA because indirect branching stacks with flattening and its runtime penalty lands directly in the hot float loop. SPLIT stays as a low-cost diversifier. CorrectnessRisk weights stay low across the board given round 1 showed clean compilation and execution with no ICE fallback.
